title: Vascular System Anatomy: Aorta, Arteries & Venous Trees
description: Study vascular system anatomy across the pulmonary and systemic circuits, tracing the aorta, carotid, mesenteric, and limb arteries with major venae cavae.
h1: Vascular System Anatomy: Aorta, Major Arteries, Veins and Capillaries
blurb: High-pressure elastic and muscular arteries branching from the aorta paired with valve-guarded veins and portal circuits returning blood to the heart.
lead: Branching from the elastic arch of the aorta down to microscopic capillary beds and valve-guarded veins, the vascular system delivers oxygen to every living cell. In this illustrated guide to vascular system anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including aortic arch, common carotid artery, subclavian artery, brachial artery—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Branching from the elastic arch of the aorta down to microscopic capillary beds and valve-guarded veins, the vascular system delivers oxygen to every living cell. The arterial and venous maps a surgeon names daily, from carotids to saphenous. Within the human body, the vascular system (Systema cardiovasculare) is situated in whole body, receives arterial perfusion via the heart, and is innervated by autonomic vasomotor.

Structurally, the aortic arch (Arcus aortae) comprises curve giving brachiocephalic, left carotid, left subclavian. Physiologically, the aortic arch distributes to head and arms. Structurally, the common carotid artery (A. carotis communis) comprises neck artery bifurcating at C4. Physiologically, the common carotid artery governs brain and face supply. Anatomically, the subclavian artery (A. subclavia) lies under clavicle to axillary artery. Physiologically, the subclavian artery governs arm supply; gives vertebral to brain. The brachial artery (A. brachialis) is upper-arm continuation. Physiologically, the brachial artery governs arm and forearm supply; BP cuff site. Structurally, the descending aorta (Aorta descendens) comprises thoracic then abdominal aorta. Physiologically, the descending aorta governs segmental branches to wall and viscera. Structurally, the coeliac trunk (Truncus coeliacus) comprises t12 branch: left gastric, splenic, hepatic. Physiologically, the coeliac trunk governs foregut supply.

Clinically, regarding the aortic arch, coarctation: hypertension above, weak femorals below. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the common carotid artery, carotid bruit = stroke risk; press on the sinus to slow the heart. In clinical pathology involving the subclavian artery, subclavian steal reverses vertebral flow on exertion. Medical evaluation of the brachial artery also notes that intra-arterial cannulation risk at elbow.

questions.question: What is the difference between arteries and veins?
questions.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it. This describes direction of flow, not oxygen content—pulmonary arteries carry less-oxygenated blood.

questions.question: What is the aorta's role in circulation?
questions.answer: The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle and supplies the systemic arterial tree through branches serving the head, trunk and limbs.

questions.question: What is the aortic arch?
questions.answer: The aortic arch is the curved part of the aorta that gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.

questions.question: Where is the subclavian artery located?
questions.answer: The subclavian artery passes beneath the clavicle and continues as the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.

questions.question: What is the function of the descending aorta?
questions.answer: The descending aorta supplies the thorax and abdomen through branches to the body wall and visceral organs.
